To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) astrocytes are able to release neurotransmitters by exocytosis of synaptic-like microvesicle (SLMVs), (ii) exocytotic events occur in submicrometric cytosolic compartments, delimited by endoplasic reticulum tubules, and (iii) Ca2+ transients in the subplasmatic membrane compartments control the exo-endocytic process.
astrocytic exocytosis of synaptic-like microvescicles proceeds with a time scale of a few hundreds of milliseconds and that this process is controlled by local subplasma membrane Ca2+ transients.

1) astrocytes can recycle synaptic-like microvesicular glutamate, 2) the recycling of synaptic-like microvesicle glutamate is fast, and 3) recycling is regulated by submicron cytoplasmic Ca2+ transients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of stimulus-secretion coupling and recycling of synaptic-like vesicles (SLVs) in astroglial cells.
the identification of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the exocytosis of SLMVs and the recycling of their content, in astrocytes and in neurons.
the elucidation of the molecular and cellular basis of Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes, a fundamental process in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
astrocytes are able to release neurotransmitters in a fast and regulated manner, and that they are able to control their exo-endocytic process with a time scale of milliseconds.
astrocytic exocytosis and endocytosis are very fast, and the exocytosis process is controlled by local subplasma membrane Ca2+ microdomain transients.

the exocytosis of synaptic-like microvescicles in astrocytes, although sharing some common features with neuronal exocytotic processes, is also endowed with peculiar properties that may allow a specific role of astrocytes in the regulation of brain signaling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
astrocytes are not only the most abundant cells in the brain, but also the fastest.
we have identified a new mechanism for the release of glutamate in astrocytes, which is fast, Ca2+-dependent, and mediated by SLMVs.
astrocytes are capable of fast synaptic-like exo-endocytic processes, and that these processes may be controlled by local Ca(2+) events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatiotemporally restricted exocytosis of SLMVs from astrocytes is mediated by local Ca2+, which in turn is released from the endoplasmic-reticulum tubules.

the exo-endocytic cycle is a highly efficient process that can be activated with a millisecond time scale in astrocytes, a feature that may have important implications in astrocytic communication and in brain signaling.
astrocytic SLMV exo-endocytic machinery is remarkably fast and efficient.
